query: A TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy has been reported in a single-phase BCC, dendritic state, with a yield strength of about 800 MPa and roughly 40% strain under lower-temperature testing, but at 1273 K it retains only 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain. For its use as an intermediate layer that transfers heat between W and CuCrZr while preserving structural integrity, what single intervention could overcome this loss of strength at elevated temperature? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the reported baseline, define the applicable thermal and mechanical boundary conditions, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, minor oxygen addition during processing of the TiVNbTa refractory HEA will promote the in situ formation of fine TiO nanoprecipitates within the BCC matrix, thereby mitigating the strength loss at elevated temperatures and enhancing its performance as an intermediate heat-transfer layer.
generation.material_initial_state: The alloy is initially a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a dendritic microstructure, exhibiting 800 MPa yield strength at lower temperatures and reduced strength (330 MPa yield strength, 423 MPa compressive strength) at 1273 K.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a carefully controlled amount of oxygen during processing (for example, by using a slightly oxygenated atmosphere or minor deliberate oxygen doping) to generate finely dispersed TiO precipitates within the alloy.
generation.conditions: The intervention is designed for operations at approximately 1273 K and under mechanical deformation up to about 30% strain, as appropriate for an intermediate layer transferring heat between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of uniformly dispersed, nanoscale TiO precipitates within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates will act as obstacles to dislocation motion (a precipitation strengthening mechanism), impeding both dislocation glide and climb at elevated temperatures. This dispersion strengthening is expected to retard high-temperature softening of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the reported baseline, the oxygen-doped alloy is predicted to retain a higher yield strength (significantly exceeding 330 MPa at 1273 K) and improved compressive strength, while maintaining acceptable ductility under high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: The current TiVNbTa alloy exhibits about 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 1273 K.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under high-temperature conditions (near 1273 K) and mechanical loading (up to ~30% strain) that mimic the operational requirements of an intermediate heat-transfer layer between W and CuCrZr.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal level of oxygen addition, the precise distribution and size of the TiO precipitates, and potential impacts on ductility or other secondary properties require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of TiVNbTa alloy samples: one group processed under standard inert atmospheric conditions (baseline) and a second group processed under a slightly oxygenated atmosphere to induce controlled TiO precipitation. Subject both groups to identical high-temperature tests at 1273 K with comparable mechanical strain conditions.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) to quantify TiO precipitate size and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase (e.g., >5% improvement) in yield and compressive strength at 1273 K relative to the inert-processed samples, or if the anticipated TiO precipitates are absent or not well-dispersed in the microstructure, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Enhanced Strength of a Mechanical Alloyed NbMoTaWVTi Refractory High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractA NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles.Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Edge-dislocation-induced ultrahigh elevated-temperature strength of HfMoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: ABSTRACTOver 150 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been proposed in the last decade. Early alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW still show an unparalleled yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 1600°C. However, RHEAs with even elevated high-temperature strength are necessary in aerospace vehicles and nuclear reactors to cope with advanced technology in the future. Here, solid-solution strengthening calculation and melting point prediction are combined to design single-phase RHEA for attaining ultrahigh strength at 1600°C. The results show that Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW alloys after fully homogeneous treatment at 2100°C for 2 h reveal a homogenous body-centered cubic phase. HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa). It is found that a plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C, which is important for raising the strength level of RHEAs at high temperatures.
